segments.title: Why a tank force cannot be rebuilt on demand
segments.summary: Britain may use its main battle tanks infrequently, yet scrapping them would leave an expensive capability to recreate and make future access dependent on allies' terms.
segments.body: Main battle tanks can look expendable in a defence review because Britain does not need them as often as some other capabilities. That low demand does not make them unnecessary. Recreating the capability after it has been discarded would be very expensive. Britain also could not assume that allies would provide tanks whenever asked. Any allied support could come with its own rules of engagement, limiting how the force could be used.

evidence.note: The transcript rejects scrapping British tanks and explains why infrequently used capabilities are expensive to regenerate and cannot simply be borrowed from allies.

segments.title: A reserve model for amphibious capability
segments.summary: The amphibious comparison offers a reserve model for costly capabilities: keep the Bay class active, hold major ships with nucleus crews and reservists, maintain them, and rehearse activation each year.
segments.body: A reserve model could preserve amphibious capability when full-time demand is low. The Bay-class ships and their Royal Fleet Auxiliary crews would stay active to keep supporting skills sharp. Major amphibious ships could enter reserve with nucleus crews and enough reservists to bring them up to strength. At least one ship would activate for an exercise each year so mobilization remained familiar. Regular maintenance would keep heavy-lift capability available when needed.

evidence.note: The transcript outlines a reserve arrangement for major amphibious ships with a nucleus crew, reservists, annual activation exercises, and maintenance.

segments.title: Keeping a reserve tank force credible
segments.summary: Britain could preserve tank numbers and the skills to use them by relying more on reservist crews and simulator training instead of abolishing the force.
segments.body: Tank capability does not have to be either fully active or eliminated. Britain already has reservist tank crews, so some of the human foundation is in place. Simulator training could help those reservists retain their skills. Keeping the vehicles while moving more of them into reserve would reduce the active commitment while preserving numbers. The force could then expand when the capability was needed.

evidence.note: The transcript argues that reservist tank crews, simulators, and maintained equipment can preserve capability without treating tanks as an all-or-nothing choice.
